title: Identifying Appeals
short: Most passages blend the appeals. Decide which one each sentence leans on most, and how they work together.
trouble: Learners look for one label for a whole passage instead of seeing how ethos, pathos and logos support each other.

blocks.html: You have met ethos, pathos and logos one at a time. Real writing mixes them, often in the same paragraph, sometimes in the same sentence. Identifying appeals means deciding what each sentence leans on most, then seeing how they work together.

head: Appeal
Ask
Clues
rows: Why should I trust this writer?
experience, fairness, admitted limits, respect for the reader
How is this meant to make me feel?
stories, vivid images, loaded words, shared values
What reasons and evidence are offered?
facts, numbers, examples, because and therefore

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: I have coached the middle school swim team for nine years.
Every summer I watch kids who never had lessons cling to the pool wall, afraid to let go.
Our town pool now offers free lessons only on weekday mornings, when most parents are at work.
When the neighboring town added evening lessons, sign-ups tripled in one season.
Let’s give every child in our town the chance to swim with confidence.

blocks.cap: A sample letter asking for evening swim lessons (its details are made up for practice). Each sentence leans on one appeal; together they make the case.

blocks.html: Label each sentence by the appeal it leans on most, then explain how the appeals support each other. Most strong passages use all three.

Appeals rarely work alone. In the swim-lesson letter, the coach’s experience (ethos) makes the scared children (pathos) believable, and the facts about schedules (logos) show the fix is practical. Seeing the teamwork tells you why the passage persuades.

blocks.title: One sentence, two appeals
blocks.q: “As a nurse who has treated dozens of bike injuries, I can tell you that a helmet turns many trips to the hospital into trips home.” Which appeal does it lean on most?
steps: “As a nurse who has treated dozens of bike injuries” builds trust: ethos.
“A helmet turns many trips to the hospital into trips home” states a claim about results, warmly phrased.
The sentence works mainly by asking us to trust her experience, so ethos leads, with some pathos in “trips home.”
blocks.a: Mostly ethos, supported by a touch of pathos.

blocks.title: Lincoln’s blend
blocks.q: Gettysburg: “The brave men, living and dead, who struggled here, have consecrated it, far above our poor power to add or detract.” What is the main appeal?
steps: It honors the soldiers and stirs reverence: pathos.
“Our poor power” is also modest, which builds ethos.
The main work is the feeling of reverence for the dead.
blocks.a: Mainly pathos, with modesty (ethos) in “our poor power.”

blocks.html: Looking for one label for a whole passage (“this speech uses pathos”). That misses how the appeals support each other, and it is rarely true. Label sentence by sentence, then say how they combine: “The writer’s experience makes the story believable, and the numbers show it isn’t a rare case.”

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: I have worked at the front desk of the public library since it opened in 2009.
On Sunday afternoons I see students sitting on the steps outside, using our wifi in the cold.
A survey of 300 patrons found that 62 percent would use the library on Sundays.
Opening four hours on Sunday would cost less than one part-time salary.

blocks.cap: Your turn: label each sentence by its main appeal, then Check.
